paras: The attempted lynching of Samuel Ewing took place on the night of Tuesday, February 22, 1881, in the eastern part of Bartholomew County, Indiana, when a masked and armed mob seized him and hanged him until he was nearly dead. The mob was trying to force him to confess to poisoning a doctor's horses, but it got no confession and left him alive. A short dispatch from Columbus, Indiana, carried the story to papers from New York to Mississippi.

According to the dispatch, a Dr. Biddinger had lost seven horses to poisoning, and the mob accused Ewing of poisoning them. None of the reports gives Ewing's race, age or occupation, or says why suspicion fell on him.

On Tuesday night a mob, "masked and armed," seized Ewing and hanged him "till he was nearly dead." Its members then stood over him with a cocked pistol, or "cocked pistols" in the New-York Tribune's version, demanding that he confess to the poisoning. In the dispatch's words, "the mob utterly failed, and abandoned the prisoner." The reports do not say where he was seized or hanged, or how many men took part.

Several versions of the dispatch closed with the line that "the agents of the law are now after the mob." No report of arrests, charges or a trial of any mob member was found, and nothing more appears about Ewing or the poisoned horses.

The story reached the press as one Columbus dispatch dated February 25, and every paper found ran nearly the same words. On February 26 it appeared in the New-York Tribune under the head "Attempt to export [extort] a confession," in the Washington Evening Star as "Cowardly work of a masked mob," and in The Daily Gazette and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer among other brief news items. The same day the Washington National Republican ran it under the head "An Ohio Mob" and printed the victim's name as "Samuel E. Wing."

Weeklies picked it up the next week: the Somerset Herald in Pennsylvania headed it "Cowardly Work," the Juniata Sentinel and Republican ran it on March 2, and the Southern Herald of Liberty, Mississippi, ran it on March 5. None of these papers mentioned race, and the only comment was in headlines such as "Cowardly work," which condemned the mob.

accounts.gist: A masked, armed mob hanged Ewing nearly to death and threatened him with a cocked pistol to force a confession of poisoning Dr. Biddinger's horses; it failed and left him, and the law was said to be after the mob.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headed the dispatch 'Cowardly work of a masked mob' and kept the line that 'the agents of the law are now after the mob.'
Most papers ran the dispatch as an unheaded or briefly headed news item; the Tribune's head stressed the extorted confession.

record_check.dossier: No article states Ewing's race; nothing in the coverage identifies him as Black.
Hanging and seizure, plus a threat with a cocked pistol to extort a confession.
Supported: hanged till nearly dead, then abandoned alive.
At least nine copies of the same dispatch in eight papers, Feb. 26 to Mar. 5, 1881.
